purpose: Pretomanid is used to treat a very serious, hard-to-cure form of tuberculosis (TB) called extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) or treatment-intolerant/non-responsive multidrug-resistant TB. It is always used in combination with two other TB medicines, bedaquiline and linezolid. This combination is sometimes called the BPaL regimen.
how_it_works: Pretomanid works by attacking and killing the bacteria that cause tuberculosis in two different ways. It damages the outer covering of the TB bacteria and also interferes with their ability to make energy, essentially starving and destroying them. Because it works differently than older TB drugs, it can fight bacteria that have become resistant to other treatments.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, and stomach upset are common. You may also experience nerve pain, numbness, or tingling in your hands and feet (peripheral neuropathy), anemia (low red blood cells causing fatigue), headache, low blood sugar, skin rash, and acne. Some patients notice changes in liver enzyme levels detected by blood tests.
warnings: This drug can cause serious liver damage — your doctor will monitor your liver with regular blood tests. It can also cause a dangerous heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, so tell your doctor about any heart conditions or other medications you take. Peripheral neuropathy (nerve damage) can be serious and may not fully go away. Pretomanid may lower male fertility and can harm an unborn baby, so effective birth control is important for both men and women during treatment. Never take pretomanid alone — it must always be used with bedaquiline and linezolid.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is one 200 mg tablet taken by mouth once a day with food. Treatment typically lasts 26 weeks (about 6 months). Always take it exactly as your doctor or pharmacist tells you, and never skip doses, as this can make the bacteria harder to treat.
